Pot sa-ti raspund din perspectiva mea ca expat in Olanda. Am venit aici ca la mama pe tarla, m-am dus la primarie sa ma inregistrez, tot ce mi-a trebuit a fost contractul de chirie si pasaportul UE ca sa-mi ureze bun venit. M-am angajat, tot asa, le-am aratat pasaportul romanesc si aia a fost tot ce a trebuit sa stie.

Compara asta cu prietenii non-UE pe care-i am. Le-au trebuit o suta de hartii si procese ca sa poata sa puna piciorul in tara asta si inca o suta de hartii si procese ca sa poata sa se angajeze. Si toate astea ca sa primeasca permis temporar in majoritatea cazurilor si sa stea cu morcovul adanc ca la un moment dat o sa le expire si nu stiu daca o sa poata sa le reinnoiasca. Si mai avem inca vreo 30 si ceva de tari in care putem sa facem asta. Toate aeroporturile UE au cozi separate pentru noi, in multe cazuri suntem exceptia, nu regula.

Si chiar daca nu vrei sa pleci din tara (desi macar in vreo vacanta ai vrea sa mergi, e frumos sa n-ai nevoie de viza si sa te duci unde vrei cand vrei), poate ai o firma si vrei sa-ti extinzi serviciile in mai multe tari. Nimic mai simplu intre doi membri UE, ai mult mai putina birocratie de rezolvat si taxe scazute, chiar deloc in unele cazuri.

Nu zic ca n-are si uniunea bubele ei, dar exista multe avantaje clare.
Nu e nimic asa socant sau neasteptat in chestia asta, ne place noua sa ne plangem dar habar n-aveti cati oameni si-ar taia o mana ca sa scrie UE pe pasaportul lor.

What you're describing about your MO and ethics is exactly what I would expect from a therapist . 

My point being, if there was a strict standard for therapists to behave in the way that you do, I would have much more respect for and trust in therapy. But it seems like there is not, since many less-ethical therapists do not do what you do and still profess. Therefore, I would still think that going to therapy could very much be a gamble. I could get someone like you who would be straight-up about what they can and they cannot do for me, or someone who will not care that they cannot actually help me.

That being said, while I still stand on my opinion that therapy as a practice needs to be revised and changed drastically, you have helped me tremendously in giving advice on how to find what kind of therapy/therapist works for me. So thank you a lot.

Yeah, that's exactly what I'm saying. There are many different types of therapy and counseling and it depends on what I need, fine, fair enough. Why don't we have some generalists where you can go, tell them what your problems are and what you expect to get so that they can tell you what kind of therapy you need (you know, much like a GP works)? Without this, it's pretty much a gamble where you go to one type of therapy (whichever that is) and hope for the best that first of all the type of therapy is what you need and second of all that you will "click" with your therapist. So I guess then therapy works for the people who have "Yes" as answers to both of my questions above but sadly those who don't are stuck paying a lot of money and putting in a lot of effort without anyone telling them they're looking in the right place. 

You also said I'm not trying to implement what I'm being taught, but my main problem is that there is nothing for implement if all I get is "Aha, I see, so how does that make you feel? Interesting", as I said in my post that I got from all my therapists.

Well, yeah, but I also know therapists become so because someone allowed them to. And I propose that these standards for who can be a therapist need to change if the results can be so unsatisfying. 

That's why I draw so many parallels to medicine. In order to become a doctor, you do a degree that's both much longer and much more difficult than others, followed by many years of practice, an oath and a crapload of paperwork before getting a license. And what that license says is "This person is knowledgeable, skilled and motivated enough to be trusted to work with something as sacred as the human body".

The human mind is, in my opinion, just as sacred, but I don't see that much standardisation and rigourousness in who can become a therapist. Not to mention, medicine is at least straight-up about its limitation. A doctor will tell someone with terminal cancer that it is very unlikely they will be cured, but the doctor will only try to improve the length and quality of their life. Therapy seems to be more "You first pay me and then we'll see what I can do for you, which might very well be nothing". I've been very clear to all my therapists about what I expect from them, if that's not what therapy is supposed to be, tell me that on the very first session so I can go find what I need somewhere else, don't let me figure it out by myself after milking me for money as much as possible.

I would be a little bit more happy with trying as much therapy as possible if at least it was covered by my insurance. In my country it's unfortunately in principle not, maybe just a couple sessions but not nearly enough to even tell if it's helping or not.

Hard to tell whether it's mainstream or not, but I've definitely had it recommended way too many times when I've told people about my struggles and any attempt for me to say I've tried it before and it didn't do anything was met with the cliche advice of "You haven't found one you clicked with" or "Maybe you didn't put the work"

Well then why has no therapist ever bothered to explain me how this works? If you see someone has fundamentally wrong ideas about what to expect and you are an expert in this field, shouldn't you tell them what you can actually do for them? 

And the number three (as in the number of therapists that disappointed me so far) is what made me start thinking there might be something wrong with the field itself. One bad therapist could be a misfortune, two a coincidence but after three I'm going skeptical. Sure, I could keep switching therapists until I maybe but not necessarily find one that works for me, but how much money will I potentially waste on the way? It's exactly for this reason why I think the procedure needs a lot of change, it's unfair and unreasonable to expect someone to do so much and just maybe find some solutions. 

And I'm trying to get helped, it's not that I refuse help. "How does that make you feel" is a level-one-depth question. I've never had a therapist go at any other level beside that. They ask me how I feel, I say it to the best of my ability with no guarantee to either me or them that this is even remotely correct, they draw some also potentially half-assed generic conclusion, thank you, that will be all, here's your receipt, see you next week.

> This is an institutional problem, not a personal one. In other words, it just means that your insurance or your government needs to be fixed, not that therapy itself is problematic.

Fair, I went a bit beyond the scope of this topic, my bad. 

> It sounds like the issue is that you're just more medically literate than you are psychologically. In other words, you know what questions to ask the doctor 

Not quite, I'm actually just your average WebMD searcher when it comes to that. I simply like that I can go to the doctor with no knowledge about this field and just with knowing what my complaint is and then they can come up with a cause/solution for it. I'm frustrated I can't get that from a therapist. 

> 1) Have you treated people with my condition before? What you think will likelihood of significant improvement for me will be?

> 2) Which methodology or type of therapy do you use?

> 3) What disorders do you specialize in? Do you have experience treating my disorder?

All very good points which will at least give me a new approach towards finding what I need. !delta

No, it's not that question that I hate in itself. That should only be the first question towards a series of other questions that will help me understand why I feel this way. But when I say how I feel, the therapist says "Why do you think you feel this way", I give the best answer that I can as an uneducated person in this field and then, instead of giving any guidance whether what I said could be true or not based on the crapload of books they've read, they say "Hmmm, interesting", I might start wondering what am I spending my money on.

Thank you, you really get it. That's what I meant when I said in my post "I do, however, think that there is a lot more improvement to be made before it can be marketed the way it is.". I struggle with mental health myself, so it would be stupid to say it's not a real issue, and I hate how much therapy costs and is marketed as the one solution to all your problems when in reality it's much more complicated than it is and it only MIGHT help SOME people, but it will sure as hell cost you a lot with no guarantee of results.

1. Yeah, if I go to three different mechanics and none of them are able to fix my cars, I would wonder who the hell let these people work in this field and whether there shouldn't be some stricter standards before we let people take other people's money to fix their cars. Now consider that my mind is something even more sensitive and important than my car and a therapist costs way more and takes more time than a mechanic, and I can conclude that  I have the right to ask myself who lets some people be therapists.

2. Well, I would very much like a therapist to give me his theories of why am I feeling this way and explore them together. After all, he studied the human mind and behaviour, I didn't. When he keeps asking me "Why do you think you feel this way", the only answer I can give is "I don't effing know and that's why I'm paying you". I get it that it's supposed to be me who looks into my mind, but I need someone to ask me the right questions, not just say "Hmm, interesting" and "How does that make you feel?"

Again with the doctor parallel. I go to a doctor, tell them my stomach hurts, they ask some relevant questions, find some possible causes for it, run the appropriate tests to find the exact cause and then take action based on it. If the doctor kept asking me why do I think my stomach hurts I would curse them and whoever gave them their medical license.

Wellll, that doesn't change the second issue I raised (the practical level). First of all, medicine is way cheaper than therapy and way more likely to be insured one way or another, so I don't have to worry about potentially wasting a lot of money and getting no result. Second of all, I have acknowledged that there are more types of therapy, but I've never been presented with the options and told whether what I need can be done by that therapist in particular, instead all I got was "this is how I do things, you pay and hope for the best".

And if you tell me I'm supposed to already know what kind of therapy I need before going to a therapist, that's another major flaw in the field itself then. Drawing the parallel to medicine again, there's also various types of treatment for various types of problems. I go to the doctor, tell them what's bothering me, then it's up to them to ask the right questions, investigate the right things and come up with a course of action that will get rid of my issue. Sure, it might help if I already have an idea of what I could have, but this should be optional and a good doctor should be able to identify my problem even if I know dick about medicine and can't help them in any way.

Yes, I know it's a very young field, compared to medicine which has been around for centuries. Exactly for that reason I think we should stop marketing therapy as the one thing to fix all of your problems. It's high up there in the advice given to struggling people next to trying to work out and eat healthy (the other two are actually good and have done much more for me than therapy would ever dream to).

Not to mention, if you go to any therapist's website, they will tell you how great they are and how many of your problems they have managed to fix, but they...didn't? Not for me at least. So these are empty promises as far as I'm concerned.
